blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 1 (Periodic Table and Periodic Properties), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Describe the contributions of Döbereiner, Newlands, Mendeleev and Lothar Meyer to the classification of elements. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Döbereiner (1829): grouped elements with similar properties into triads (groups of three). The atomic weight of the middle element was roughly the average of the other two, e.g. Li (7), Na (23), K (39): (7 + 39) ÷ 2 = 23.

Newlands (1864): first observed periodicity in the 62 known elements. Arranged by increasing atomic masses, every eighth element resembled the first in properties, and he grouped them accordingly.

Mendeleev (1869): considered the father of the periodic table. He arranged 63 elements in eight vertical columns by increasing atomic mass, putting elements with similar properties in vertical groups. He left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their atomic masses and properties, which proved accurate when the elements were found.

Lothar Meyer (1869): plotted a graph between atomic weights and atomic volumes of elements; his curves also showed periodicity.

book_ref.quote: Over time, more elements were discovered, prompting scientists to organize them systematically

blocks.prompt: 2 How did Moseley's work change the basis of the periodic table? State the Modern Periodic Law and explain it with an example. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Moseley's work (1913): Moseley determined the exact atomic numbers of known elements using X-ray emission. He arranged the elements by atomic numbers instead of atomic masses, which resolved the flaws and discrepancies of Mendeleev's table, and modified the periodic law.

Modern Periodic Law: "The physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers."

Explanation: The atomic number is the number of protons in an atom. The law is the cornerstone of the periodic table: when elements are arranged by increasing atomic numbers, elements with similar properties appear at certain intervals. For example, sodium, potassium and cesium show many physical and chemical characteristics similar to lithium, as they are all in the same group.

Within a group and a period the properties vary systematically because the number of protons in the nucleus increases gradually and new electron shells are added.

book_ref.quote: This significant breakthrough led Moseley to modify the Periodic Law

blocks.prompt: 3 Describe the main features of the modern periodic table. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Presently 118 elements are arranged in ascending order of their atomic numbers.
2. There are seven horizontal rows called periods and eighteen vertical columns called groups. (Older versions had 8 vertical groups divided into eight A-groups and ten B-groups.)
3. Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of valence electrons; their physical properties change gradually from top to bottom.
4. Elements in a period show a gradual change in properties from left to right.
5. Besides groups and periods, the elements are also grouped into blocks (s, p, d, f), families and categories (metals, non-metals, metalloids) to make understanding easier.

book_ref.quote: The classification of elements in the modern periodic table helps in the easier understanding of their properties

blocks.prompt: 4 Explain the classification of elements into metals, non-metals and metalloids. Describe the position of each with respect to the stair-step line. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Metals: elements which tend to lose electrons to form positive ions, e.g. iron, copper, gold and silver.

Non-metals: elements which tend to gain electrons to form negative ions, e.g. chlorine, sulfur and phosphorus.

Metalloids (semimetals): show some properties of metals and some of non-metals; they separate metals and non-metals on the table.

Stair-step line: Most periodic tables have a stair-step line that begins at boron (B) and extends down to polonium (Po), including Si, Ge, As, Sb and Te.
• Elements to the left of the line are metals.
• Elements just to the right of the line are metalloids.
• Elements to the far right of the table are non-metals.
• Hydrogen, the first element, is the exception: it is on the left but is not a metal.

book_ref.quote: Elements can be broadly classified as metals, nonmetals and metalloids

blocks.prompt: 5 What are blocks of the periodic table? Describe the s, p, d and f blocks and the importance of knowing the block of an element. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Elements are classified into blocks on the basis of the subshell that contains their valence electrons.

s-block: the first two groups (1 and 2); their valence electrons are in s subshells.
p-block: the elements of groups 13 to 18, including the inert gases of the last group.
d-block: the transition elements in the middle of the table.
f-block: the two series at the bottom of the table, the lanthanides and actinides.

Importance: Knowing the block of an element gives valuable information about its characteristics, chemical reactivity, oxidation states, electron filling and other properties such as electronegativity and ionization energy.

book_ref.quote: Elements in the periodic table can be classified based on the subshells containing their valence electrons

blocks.prompt: 6 Describe the alkali metals and alkaline earth metals, giving the reason for their names, examples and properties. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Alkali metals (group 1) produce alkalis with water and alkaline earth metals (group 2) are found in the earth and form alkalis.

book_ref.quote: Sodium and potassium are notable examples of these elements

rows: Group 1 of the periodic table.
Group 2 of the periodic table.
Named because they produce alkalis when they react with water.
Named because they are found mainly in the earth and form alkalis.
Members: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr; e.g. sodium, potassium.
Members: Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra; e.g. calcium, magnesium.
One valence electron.
Two valence electrons, so divalent.
Low densities and relatively low melting points.
Metallic solids, harder and denser than alkali metals.
Low ionization energies; the most reactive metals.
Easily oxidized; high thermal and electrical conductivities.

blocks.prompt: 7 Describe the transition elements, chalcogens, halogens and noble gases as families of the periodic table. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Transition elements: the largest family, in the middle of the table; four series of d-block elements plus the lanthanides and actinides (f-block). They have high thermal and electrical conductivities, high melting points, high density and variable oxidation states, and mostly form coloured compounds. Members include Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn.

Chalcogens (group 16): named because most ores of copper (Greek chalkos) are oxides or sulfides. Oxygen and sulphur are non-metals, Se, Te and Po are metalloids and livermorium is a metal.

Halogens (group 17): non-metals (F, Cl, Br, I, At, Ts). Halogen means "salt-former" because they easily react with alkali and alkaline earth metals to form stable halide salts. They are highly reactive, have high electron affinities and easily accept one electron to complete their outermost shell.

Noble gases (group 18): He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn, Og at the extreme right. With a complete outermost shell they are almost unreactive and monoatomic. Some compounds are known, e.g. XePtF₆, so the name inert gases was changed to noble gases.

book_ref.quote: The term “halogen” means “salt-former”

blocks.prompt: 8 Explain how the period number, group number and block of an element are related to its electronic configuration. Write the configuration of an element of period 3 and group 13. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Period number: indicates the principal quantum number n, i.e. the number of electron shells around the nucleus. An element in the 3rd period has three shells and its valence electrons are in the 3rd shell.

Block: the specific subshell of the valence electrons depends on the block (azimuthal quantum number). An element of period 3 in the s-block has its valence electrons in the 3s subshell.

Group number: indicates the number of valence electrons. An element in period 3 and group 2 (s-block) has two valence electrons in 3s; this element is magnesium.

Example, period 3 and group 13: group 13 means 3 valence electrons; period 3 means three shells, so the 3 valence electrons are in the 3rd shell:
1s² (1st shell)   2s² 2p⁶ (2nd shell)   3s² 3p¹ (3rd shell)

Thus the position of an element explains its electronic configuration, which is essential for understanding its chemical behaviour.

book_ref.quote: Understanding the periodic arrangement of elements provides an explanation of an element’s electronic configuration

blocks.prompt: 9 Define atomic radius. Name the factors affecting it and explain its variation across a period and down a group. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: The atomic radius is a measure of the size of an atom; it is half of the distance between two identical atoms bonded together. It can vary with the type of bond (covalent, metallic, van der Waals) or the state of the atom, and is measured in picometres (pm) or angstroms (Å).

Factors: atomic number, effective nuclear charge and shielding effect of inner electrons.

Across a period (left to right): atomic radius generally decreases. The nuclear charge increases while no new shell is added, so the electron cloud is pulled closer to the nucleus.

Down a group (top to bottom): atomic radius increases. Additional electron shells are added, and the greater shielding makes the atom larger; the increase in nuclear charge is outweighed.

book_ref.quote: The atomic radius is typically measured in picometers (pm) or Angstroms (Å)

blocks.prompt: 10 What is ionic radius? Explain why a cation is smaller and an anion larger than the parent atom, and describe the trends of ionic radius in the periodic table. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Ionic radius: a measure of the size of an ion in a crystal lattice; the distance from the nucleus of the ion to its outermost electron shell, measured in pm or Å.

Cation: When an atom loses one or more electrons to become a positive ion, it becomes smaller than the neutral atom. The loss of electrons reduces electronic repulsion and the remaining electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus.

Anion: When an atom gains one or more electrons, it becomes larger than the neutral atom. The added electrons increase electronic repulsion, the nuclear pull on the electrons decreases and the electron cloud expands.

Across a period: the ionic radius of cations decreases, because the increasing nuclear charge pulls the electrons closer; the ionic radius of anions also decreases for the same reason.

Down a group: both cations and anions increase in size, because the principal quantum number n increases, adding electron shells. The outermost electrons are farther from the nucleus, outweighing the increased nuclear charge.

book_ref.quote: The ionic radius is a measure of the size of an ion in a crystal lattice

blocks.prompt: 11 Define first, second and third ionization energies, taking calcium as the example. How many ionization energies can an element have? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
First ionization energy (ΔHᵢ₁): the energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of atoms of the element in the gaseous state to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.
Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻   ΔHᵢ₁ = 494 kJ mol⁻¹
Ca(g) → Ca⁺(g) + e⁻   ΔHᵢ₁ = 590 kJ mol⁻¹

Second ionization energy (ΔHᵢ₂): the energy needed to remove a second electron from each ion in a mole of gaseous 1+ ions.
Ca⁺(g) → Ca²⁺(g) + e⁻   ΔHᵢ₂ = 1150 kJ mol⁻¹

Third ionization energy (ΔHᵢ₃): the energy needed to remove a third electron from each ion in a mole of gaseous 2+ ions.
Ca²⁺(g) → Ca³⁺(g) + e⁻   ΔHᵢ₃ = 4940 kJ mol⁻¹

Number of ionization energies: an element can have several ionization energies; the exact number equals its atomic number (one for each electron).

book_ref.quote: The energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of atoms of the element in the gaseous state

blocks.prompt: 12 The first, second and third ionization energies of calcium are 590, 1150 and 4940 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate (i) the energy needed to convert 2.5 mol of Ca(g) into Ca²⁺(g), and (ii) the energy needed to convert 0.5 mol of Ca(g) into Ca³⁺(g). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Successive ionization energies add up: to reach Ca²⁺ remove two electrons, to reach Ca³⁺ remove three; then multiply by the moles.

book_ref.quote: Removal of a third electron from each ion in a mole of gaseous 2+ ions corresponds to the 3rd ionization energy

steps: (i) Per mole, Ca(g) → Ca²⁺(g) + 2e⁻ needs ΔHᵢ₁ + ΔHᵢ₂ = 590 + 1150 = 1740 kJ mol⁻¹
(ii) Per mole, Ca(g) → Ca³⁺(g) + 3e⁻ needs 590 + 1150 + 4940 = 6680 kJ mol⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 13 The first ionization energy of sodium is 494 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the energy required to convert 4.6 g of gaseous sodium atoms into Na⁺(g) ions. (Molar mass of Na = 23 g mol⁻¹) (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Change the mass to moles, then multiply by the energy per mole.

book_ref.quote: to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions is known as 1st ionization energy

steps: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻   ΔHᵢ₁ = 494 kJ mol⁻¹
Moles of Na = mass ÷ molar mass = 4.6 ÷ 23 = 0.2 mol

blocks.prompt: 14 Nitrogen has a higher first ionization energy than oxygen although oxygen has the greater nuclear charge. Explain this with the help of electronic arrangement and spin-pair repulsion. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Electronic configurations:
₇N = 1s² 2s² 2px¹ 2py¹ 2pz¹   ΔHᵢ₁ = 1403 kJ mol⁻¹
₈O = 1s² 2s² 2px² 2py¹ 2pz¹   ΔHᵢ₁ ≈ 1314 kJ mol⁻¹

Electronic arrangement: Half-filled and completely filled orbitals are more stable, so ionization energy is higher when the electron has to be removed from a half-filled or fully-filled subshell. Nitrogen has a half-filled 2p subshell (2p³). Although nitrogen has one unit less positive charge in its nucleus than oxygen, the extra stability of its half-filled subshell makes it difficult to remove an electron from N.

Spin-pair repulsion: When two electrons are spin-paired in the same orbital, they repel each other, so one of them is slightly easier to remove. Oxygen has two spin-paired electrons in one 2p orbital; removing one of them needs relatively less energy. Nitrogen has three unpaired 2p electrons; removing one needs more energy because there is no spin-pair repulsion.

Hence the first ionization energy of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen.

book_ref.quote: Nitrogen (N) has three unpaired electrons in its 2p orbitals

blocks.prompt: 15 Define first and second electron affinity. Explain with equations why the first electron affinity of oxygen is negative but the second is positive, and find the net enthalpy change for forming the oxide ion. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
First electron affinity (ΔH°ₑₐ₁): the enthalpy change when 1 mole of electrons is added to 1 mole of gaseous atoms to form 1 mole of gaseous uni-negative ions under standard conditions. Example:
Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g)   ΔH°ₑₐ₁ = −348.8 kJ mol⁻¹
This energy is released when 6.02 × 10²³ gaseous Cl atoms become Cl⁻(g) ions; since energy is released the sign is negative.

Second electron affinity (ΔH°ₑₐ₂): the energy required to add electrons to 1 mole of uni-negative gaseous ions to form 1 mole of gaseous 2− ions under standard conditions.

Oxygen: when the first electron is added to a neutral oxygen atom, energy is released:
O(g) + e⁻ → O⁻(g)   ΔH°ₑₐ₁ = −141 kJ mol⁻¹
But energy is absorbed on adding the second electron to the uni-negative O⁻ ion:
O⁻(g) + e⁻ → O²⁻(g)   ΔH°ₑₐ₂ = +798 kJ mol⁻¹

Net change for O(g) + 2e⁻ → O²⁻(g):
ΔH°ₑₐ₁ + ΔH°ₑₐ₂ = (−141) + (+798) = +657 kJ mol⁻¹

book_ref.quote: The second electron affinity, ΔH°ₑₐ₂ is the amount of energy required to add electrons

blocks.prompt: 16 The first and second electron affinities of oxygen are −141 and +798 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the enthalpy change when 0.4 mol of gaseous oxygen atoms are converted into O²⁻(g) ions. Is energy released or absorbed? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Add the two electron affinities to get the change per mole of O²⁻, then multiply by the moles; the sign tells released (−) or absorbed (+).

book_ref.quote: The net enthalpy change for the formation of the oxide ion (O²⁻) can be calculated

steps: Per mole: ΔH = ΔH°ₑₐ₁ + ΔH°ₑₐ₂ = (−141) + (+798) = +657 kJ mol⁻¹
The sign is positive, so energy is absorbed

blocks.prompt: 17 The first electron affinity of chlorine is −348.8 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the energy released when 1.505 × 10²³ gaseous chlorine atoms are converted into Cl⁻(g) ions. (One mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ atoms.) (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Turn the number of atoms into moles, then multiply by the energy released per mole.

book_ref.quote: This is amount of energy released when 6.02 × 10²³ atoms of chlorine

steps: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g)   ΔH°ₑₐ₁ = −348.8 kJ mol⁻¹
blocks.final_answer: 87.2 kJ of energy is released (ΔH = −87.2 kJ)

blocks.prompt: 18 Define electronegativity and describe Pauling's scale. Explain the periodic trends of electronegativity in groups and periods, and why metals are electropositive. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: Electronegativity is the power of an atom to attract a shared pair of electrons toward itself in a molecule.

Pauling scale: Linus Pauling developed a scale of dimensionless electronegativity values ranging from just below one for alkali metals to a maximum of four for fluorine. Higher values mean a stronger attraction for electrons.

Across a period: electronegativity increases from left to right because the nuclear charge increases and the size decreases; e.g. Li in period 2 is 1.0 and F is 4.0.

Down a group: electronegativity decreases from top to bottom because the size increases by addition of shells and the shielding effect increases; e.g. in the halogens it decreases from fluorine (4.0) to iodine (2.5): F > Cl > Br > I.

Metals and non-metals: metals, on the left of the table, have lower electronegativity values than non-metals. Hence metals are relatively electropositive and non-metals electronegative.

book_ref.quote: Higher electronegativity values signify a stronger attraction for electrons

blocks.prompt: 19 What is metallic character? Explain its variation across a period and down a group of the periodic table. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Metallic character: the tendency of an element to lose electrons. Elements on the left of the table readily lose their outermost electrons to achieve a noble gas configuration and form positive ions (metals); elements on the right, especially the right corner, tend to gain electrons and form negative ions (non-metals). Metallic character therefore largely depends on the valence shell electronic configuration.

Across a period: nuclear charge increases while atomic size decreases, so the valence electrons are attracted more strongly. The electron cloud is pulled closer to the nucleus, the atom loses electrons with more difficulty, and metallic character decreases from left to right.

Down a group: atomic size and shielding effect increase, reducing the nuclear attraction on the valence electrons. Losing electrons becomes easier, so metallic character increases and the element becomes more reactive. Hence cesium is far more reactive and electropositive than sodium or lithium.

book_ref.quote: Hence one can conclude that the metallic character of an element largely depends on its valence shell electronic configuration

blocks.prompt: 20 Describe the burning of sodium and magnesium in oxygen. Give balanced equations, the conditions for sodium oxide and sodium peroxide, the flame colours and one use of magnesium. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Sodium: Sodium burns in oxygen with a golden yellow flame to produce a white solid mixture of sodium oxide and sodium peroxide. It reacts vigorously with oxygen in open air to form the peroxide:
2Na(s) + O₂(g) → Na₂O₂(s)
Under special conditions such as limited O₂ or high temperature, sodium oxide is formed:
4Na(s) + O₂(g) → 2Na₂O(s)
Because of this reactivity, sodium is kept under kerosene oil to prevent its reaction with air.

Magnesium: Magnesium burns in oxygen with an intense white flame to give white solid magnesium oxide:
2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s)
Use: magnesium powder burns very rapidly with an intense white flame, so it is used in fireworks and S.O.S. flares.

book_ref.quote: Sodium burns in oxygen with a golden yellow flame to produce a white solid mixture

blocks.prompt: 21 What are oxides? Define amphoteric oxides and explain the amphoteric nature of aluminium oxide with equations. Also show with equations that SiO₂ and SO₂ behave as acidic oxides towards bases. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Oxides: binary compounds formed by the reaction of oxygen with other elements. They are classified as neutral, amphoteric, basic or acidic according to their characteristics.

Amphoteric oxides: oxides that can react with both acids and bases, i.e. they can behave as an acid or a base depending on the conditions.

Aluminium oxide: Al₂O₃ is insoluble in water but reacts with both:
• with hydrochloric acid, forming aluminium chloride and water:
Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O
• with sodium hydroxide, forming sodium aluminate and water:
Al₂O₃(s) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂Al₂O₄ + H₂O(l)

Acidic behaviour towards bases: acidic oxides of non-metals are held together by covalent bonds and react with bases.
SiO₂(s) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SiO₃(aq) + H₂O(l)
SO₂(g) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₃(aq) + H₂O(l)
Silicon dioxide is an acidic oxide because it reacts with bases.

book_ref.quote: The classification of oxides is done into neutral, amphoteric and basic or acidic based on their characteristics

blocks.prompt: 22 Distinguish between hydration and hydrolysis of the chlorides of period 3. Explain with equations and pH values why NaCl and MgCl₂ give nearly neutral solutions while AlCl₃ and SiCl₄ give acidic solutions. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Hydration (neutral chlorides): At the start of period 3, the chlorides of sodium and magnesium do not react with water. In solution, the positive metal ions and negative chloride ions become surrounded by water molecules; these are hydrated ions and the process is hydration. The solution is neutral, pH close to 7:
NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)   (pH = 7)
MgCl₂(s) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq)   (pH = 6.5)
Group 1 and group 2 chlorides are also neutral with few exceptions.

Hydrolysis (acidic chlorides): From aluminium to sulphur, the chlorides react with water to make an acidic solution with pH less than 7; this is hydrolysis. The hydrated Al³⁺ ion causes a water molecule to lose an H⁺ ion, which turns the solution acidic:
AlCl₃(s) + 3H₂O(l) → Al(OH)₃(s) + 3HCl(aq)
SiCl₄(l) + 2H₂O(l) → SiO₂(s) + 4HCl(aq)
PCl₃(l) + 3H₂O(l) → H₃PO₃ + 3HCl(aq)
The HCl formed makes these solutions acidic.

book_ref.quote: These chlorides show characteristic behavior when we add them into water

blocks.prompt: 23 Describe the trend in bonding in the oxides and chlorides of period 3 elements. Give the reason for the trend. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Across period 3 the oxides and chlorides change from ionic to covalent.

book_ref.quote: This transition is a result of the increasing electronegativity and decreasing ionic character

rows: Oxides (e.g. Na₂O) have more ionic character.
Oxides (e.g. SO₂) are more covalent.
Oxides exist as giant ionic lattices.
Oxides such as SO₂ exist as covalent molecules.
Strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions.
Weak intermolecular forces between molecules.
Chlorides (e.g. NaCl) are predominantly ionic.
Chlorides (e.g. PCl₅) are covalent.
Large electronegativity difference with O or Cl.
Electronegativity difference with the halogen decreases, so covalent character increases.

blocks.prompt: 24 Define oxidation number. Explain the variation of oxidation numbers of period 3 elements in their oxides and chlorides. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: The oxidation number (oxidation state) of an atom is the formal charge on that atom in a molecule or ion. In ionic compounds it is the charge which appears on the ions.

Period 3: The oxidation number of a period 3 element in its oxide or chloride equals the number of electrons used for bonding. It is always positive because oxygen and chlorine are more electronegative than any of these elements. The highest value matches the group number (total valence electrons).
• Oxides: increases from +1 in Na (Na₂O) to +6 in S (SO₃): Na +1, Mg +2 (MgO), Al +3 (Al₂O₃), Si +4 (SiO₂), P +5 (P₄O₁₀) or +3 (P₄O₆), S +6 (SO₃) or +4 (SO₂).
• Chlorides: increases from +1 in Na (NaCl) to +5 in P (PCl₅): Mg +2 (MgCl₂), Al +3 (AlCl₃), Si +4 (SiCl₄), P +5 or +3 (PCl₃), S +2 (SCl₂).

Variable oxidation numbers: phosphorus and sulphur show several oxidation numbers because they can expand their octet by exciting electrons into empty 3d orbitals. In SO₂ sulphur is +4 because only four electrons are used for bonding; in SO₃ it is +6 because all six are used.

book_ref.quote: Let’s examine the oxidation numbers in oxides and chlorides of the third period

blocks.prompt: 25 Taking O as −2, Cl as −1 and H as +1, calculate the oxidation number of (i) Al in Al₂O₃, (ii) P in PCl₃, (iii) S in SCl₂ and (iv) S in H₂SO₃. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: In a neutral compound the oxidation numbers add up to zero; let the unknown be x and solve.

book_ref.quote: Table 1.2: Oxidation Numbers in Oxides and Chlorides of 3rd Period elements

blocks.final_answer: Al = +3, P = +3, S in SCl₂ = +2, S in H₂SO₃ = +4
